families.s: HSE prevention of work-related violence in retail
families.t: abuse, threats, assault, robbery, age-restricted sales, lone work, risk assessment, design, procedures, reporting and support
f: Retail employers have a legal duty to protect workers from work-related violence.
Work-related violence includes physical attacks, threats, intimidation and verbal abuse.
A risk assessment should determine whether violence is a problem and what improvements are needed.
Violence procedures should form part of the wider health and safety system.
High-risk situations can include refusing age-restricted sales, handling cash and lone work.
Controls can include layout changes, barriers, staffing, communication, training and safe exit arrangements.
Incidents should be reported and reviewed, including those that do not cause injury.
Affected workers should receive appropriate support after incidents.
families.g: Retail violence risk depends on location and opening hours, customer interaction and sales policy, cash and valuables, lone work and staffing, layout, history, reporting and worker support.

families.s: HSE legal and proportionate risk-management basics for leisure activities
families.t: employers, self-employed, volunteers, premises control, workers, participants, spectators, equipment, regulation and proportionate controls
f: Workplace health and safety law applies to employers and self-employed people operating leisure activities.
They should do what is reasonably practicable to protect workers and others affected by the work.
People protected can include volunteer coaches, club members, visiting teams and spectators.
Volunteers without employees are not generally employers under the Act.
Anyone controlling non-domestic premises may still have duties to keep premises, equipment and substances safe.
Genuine risks should be minimised without unnecessarily preventing beneficial leisure activities.
Local authorities normally enforce leisure-sector health and safety law.
HSE may enforce where local authorities control facilities or where leisure takes place in education or defence premises.
families.g: Leisure duty and risk depend on employment status, control of premises and equipment, participants and spectators, activity, regulator, contractors and the proportionality of controls.

families.s: HSE safe management of amateur sports clubs
families.t: club duties, volunteers, premises, equipment, playing surfaces, spectators, pedestrian routes, electrical safety, emergencies and first aid
f: Health and safety law should not be a barrier to community amateur sport.
Employers and self-employed club organisers must protect employees and other people affected by work activities.
People controlling clubhouses or playing fields should keep premises and supplied equipment safe so far as reasonably practicable.
Sports equipment under club control should be checked and stored safely.
Playing surfaces and spectator areas should be maintained and obvious collision hazards managed.
Entrances, exits, pedestrian routes and vehicle circulation should be controlled.
Outdoor electrical supplies and temporary structures require appropriate precautions.
Clubs should plan alarms, first aid, emergency access and contingencies.
families.g: Sports-club risk depends on legal control, premises and playing surface, equipment and structures, participants and spectators, vehicles and electricity, weather, competence and emergency planning.

families.s: HSE swimming-pool operator duties and risk assessment
families.t: operator duties, workers, pool users, risk assessment, facility type, operating procedures, supervision, competence and review
f: Swimming-pool operators must protect workers and pool users.
There are no pool-specific health and safety statutes replacing general workplace duties.
Operators should complete suitable and sufficient risk assessments.
Safety measures should be selected for the risks of the particular pool.
HSE's pool guidance applies to public-use facility types defined by the relevant British Standard.
The guidance may apply to pools in non-conventional settings depending on circumstances.
Pool operating procedures should reflect the whole facility and its activities.
Arrangements should be reviewed when the facility, activities, users, staffing or equipment change.
families.g: Pool-management risk depends on pool design and depth, users and activities, staffing and supervision, water treatment, plant and equipment, operating procedures, competence and emergency response.

families.s: HSE lifeguard, on-call rescue and first-aid competence for swimming pools
families.t: supervision need, lifeguard numbers, on-call staff, immediate response, rescue, CPR, first aid, qualifications and competence
f: HSE does not prescribe a single lifeguard number for every pool.
The need for constant poolside supervision should be determined by risk assessment.
A pool-specific assessment should determine the number of lifeguards where they are required.
If constant supervision is not required, trained staff should be on call and able to respond immediately.
Relevant staff should be trained in pool rescue.
Relevant staff should be trained in CPR techniques.
Suitable first-aid competence should be available whenever the pool is in use.
A recognised current qualification can demonstrate competence, although the law does not mandate a named course.
families.g: Pool-rescue risk depends on facility and activity, visibility and blind spots, user numbers and capability, staffing, response time, rescue equipment, competence and emergency procedures.
